questions: Are you fully aware and able to remember everything while the movements occur?
Did the movements begin suddenly, within hours or a few days?
Do the movements completely stop when you are asleep?
Can you voluntarily suppress them, even briefly?
Do you feel an uncomfortable urge or inner tension before a movement that is relieved by performing it?
Are the movements brief, stereotyped episodes that recur in much the same pattern each time?
Do the movements become less frequent when you are distracted?
Have you started or increased any medication in the weeks before this began?
Have you taken an antipsychotic, anti-nausea medication, antidepressant, stimulant, levodopa, or recreational drug recently?
Have you had similar movements in the past?
Do you have weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, facial drooping, vision loss, or severe imbalance?
Do any of the affected limbs become fixed in a painful or abnormal position?
Have you recently had a fever, infection, head injury, or severe illness?
Are the movements consistently worse on one side of the body?
Does anyone in your family have similar involuntary movements or unexplained early cognitive decline?
Are you pregnant or within a year after giving birth?

dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Acute hemichorea–hemiballismus caused by an ischemic infarction of the contralateral lentiform nucleus, most consistent with a middle cerebral artery territory stroke.

ALTERNATIVE: Acute post-stroke chorea from an anterior cerebral artery territory infarction.

ALTERNATIVE: Focal motor seizure or epilepsia partialis continua presenting with abnormal limb movements.

ALTERNATIVE: Drug-induced or metabolic chorea, considered unlikely given the history and normal laboratory results.
